When someone says that you have been curt with them, they are not saying that you were brief—they are saying that you were rude.

Bedbugs don’t just live in beds. They can be in sofas, chairs, dressers and even your luggage. If you have bed bugs in your home, you could bring them with you when you travel or vice versa. Bed bugs are not a sign of uncleanliness; they are just opportunists who hitchhike from place to place on people, luggage and other items. When choosing where to stay during vacations or business trips, you want to find a place that is clean and comfortable, but also free of bed bugs. This is important because it’s difficult to get rid of bed bugs once they’ve infested a room.

The word oeuvre is often used to refer to a body of work. The French word for work is travail, and this word has been adopted into English with a slightly different meaning. In English, travail refers to labor pains or agonies, which are certainly a type of work. The French word oeuvre (pronounced "oe-vruh") means work in the sense of an artistic creation; the term is most commonly applied to paintings or sculptures. Oeuvres can also be literary works such as poems or novels. A writer's oeuvre would include all of his or her published writings.

For biologists, menopause has always been something of a mystery. While the explanation for human menopause is still not clear, we now know that chimpanzee females also experience menopause and they are our closest living relative. The researchers behind this study found that older female chimps continue to reproduce until their deaths; they just have lower reproductive rates than younger adults. In fact, the average age at which a chimp becomes infertile (50 years) is similar to humans. So if you're 30-something and feeling old, take comfort in the fact that you've got decades before you hit menopause!

A lot of this is just the usual suspects complaining about "neoliberalism", but I think it's worth thinking through. If you believe that markets are fundamentally fair and that people who get ahead deserve their success, then you don't really have any reason to worry about losers; they can always improve themselves or change careers if necessary. On the other hand, if you believe that the game is rigged in favor of the powerful and that market outcomes are often unfair, then you're going to be much more worried about protecting those who lose out from the changes driven by globalization.

Historically, luxury fashion has been about a small group of elite brands that offer exceptional quality and craftsmanship. In fact, it was said that Cleopatra crushed carmine beetles for her lipstick and she applied them with an applicator made from seaweed. The lipstick color varied according to social class: red for the upper class, dark purple for middle class women and light tint of brown or pale pink for the lower classes. Queen Elizabeth I also wore lipstick and so did Queen Victoria during her reign.

The word congenial has been around in English since at least 1580. It comes from the Latin word congenium, which means “born with,” and its original meaning was “born together.” In English it came to mean “agreeable” or “suitable.” A person who is agreeable is someone whose company you enjoy; a suitable person is one who fits well into his or her surroundings. If something is suitable for an occasion, then it’s appropriate for that particular time and place.

State courts in the 1850s were the battleground on which arguments about race, slavery, federalism, and constitutional interpretation were fought. In one of these cases—Lemmon v. The People (1852)—the highest court in New York took up the question whether slaves who had escaped to that state were free. The case was a difficult one because, although slavery had been abolished in New York, the state’s laws also forbade the harboring of fugitive slaves. The judges faced a choice between allowing slaveowners to reclaim their human “property” as the Constitution required or upholding state law and New York’s policy against slavery.

The word humbug has been around in English for a long time. It started life as slang, then became more widely used and respectable. It was first recorded in the middle of the 18th century and it originally meant 'deception' or 'imposture'. Samuel Johnson thought that this use came from the Scots language word hambog (meaning 'hoax'), but the truth is not known for certain. The second sense of humbug - meaning 'nonsense' - appeared at about the same time. This may have come from a shortening of the original phrase 'humbugging nonsense', which was a common expression in the early part of the 19th century. By the end of the 19th century, humbug had become widely accepted as standard English.

A friend of mine who is a professional counselor once told me that she always advises couples never to use the word “always” or “never” when discussing their relationship. “You never listen!” is an example of one such phrase. The reason for this advice is because it’s almost always not true that someone “never listens.” They may have missed something you said once or twice, but they don’t literally NEVER listen. Similarly, it’s very rare that a person ALWAYS does or says something. If you want your partner to be more attentive to you, using those words will likely only make them defensive and less willing to hear what you are saying.

Traumatic brain injuries can leave people unable to move or speak. Their injuries prevented messages from the brain from reaching the body, but the implanted sensors recorded signals coming from an area of the brain that controls movement. This allowed the participants to respond to questions with “yes” or “no.” The study’s authors say this is only the beginning for the technology.

Have you heard of Gresham’s Law? It is an economic principle that states bad money drives out good. The principle was named after Sir Thomas Gresham, who worked as a financial agent for King Henry VIII and Queen Elizabeth I in the 16th century. Gresham observed that when England tried to mint new coins with less silver content than older ones, the public would hoard the old coins and spend only the newer ones. In other words, people preferred holding on to the more valuable money while spending the cheaper stuff. This same phenomenon can be seen today in the way we use different currencies at various times.

French, by most accounts the world’s sexiest language, is under assault. In the suburbs of Paris, on the streets of Abidjan in Côte d’Ivoire, in the clubs of Kinshasa, and even in the halls of the Académie Française, French speakers are mixing African slang into their everyday speech. Linguists call this creolization: the process by which two languages merge to create a new one. It happened in the Caribbean when slaves blended French with English and West African tongues; now it’s happening again as millions of Africans use French to communicate across national boundaries.

To write about the past is to discover that it was once present. That is the most obvious reason why a poet who writes about the present, as Tranströmer does, has a better chance of remaining present himself. He has not yet been engulfed by nostalgia or condescension, two of history’s great modes. (The third, wishful thinking, belongs in science fiction.) There are other reasons too. A poet who writes about the present may be more likely to find readers living there, since what they have in common with him will seem more important than their differences. And he may also be less likely to make his poetry seem like a special language, an idiom set apart from ordinary usage.

In 2015, while studying the face recognition skills of chimps at the Kyoto University Primate Research Institute in Japan, researchers noticed something peculiar. One chimp seemed to remember people he had met many years before. The research team decided to conduct an experiment. They showed the chimp photographs of human faces and recorded which ones he looked at for longer than three seconds. The images included humans he knew from his younger days, as well as new acquaintances. He was also shown pictures of familiar and unfamiliar chimps. In all cases, the animal looked at the photos of those he knew for a significantly longer period of time. The results suggest that chimps can recognize and remember individual faces even after a quarter century has passed since they last saw them.

When I began my teaching career in 1980, I taught in the public schools. As an English teacher, I was assigned to teach American Literature, which included the study of Puritan writers like Jonathan Edwards and Anne Bradstreet. The latter’s poem, “Upon the Burning of our House,” was one of the most popular poems we studied. It is a reflection on how all that we possess can be taken away from us by circumstances beyond our control. Bradstreet ends her poem with these lines: “There’s wealth enough; I need no more./ Farewell, my pelf, farewell my store.” The word “pelf” means money or riches. So she is saying goodbye to all her earthly possessions.

The word dhow comes from an Arabic word meaning 'boat' or 'ship'. Dhows are sailing boats with one or more masts, and have been used in the Middle East for centuries. They were originally designed to carry heavy loads, and were used for trade between India and East Africa. Their design has evolved over time, but they still retain their traditional lateen rig (a triangular sail that is fixed at its upper end) and characteristic curved bow. They can be up to 30 metres long, and are usually made out of wood. Traditionally built dhows are still very much a part of life in countries bordering the Persian Gulf, although fibreglass versions are now commonplace.

How does a geographer study the internet? As part of the “Spatial Turn” in humanities and social science, more and more researchers are studying digital spaces, but their methods are still evolving. In this talk I discuss how a geography-informed approach to studying the internet can provide new insights into online interactions. I present some initial results from my project on Twitter geography, including visualizations of tweets about the 2014 World Cup that show how different regions of the world used the same event in very different ways. Finally, I discuss my current work using Google Maps as an ethnographic site to explore the spatial practices of mapping and map use.

It also has infinite gravity. There is no reason to believe that the Democrats will not take a page from the Republicans and vote on impeachment articles in the House, send them over to the Senate, and then refuse to do anything further with it. The Constitution does not require the Senate to hold a trial at all; the House can simply refer an article of impeachment to the Senate, and leave it up to them whether to try or not. And there's nothing in the Constitution requiring that a two-thirds majority be needed to convict someone on any given article -- they could very well split the articles into smaller groups, so that a simple majority would be enough to convict on one article, but not necessarily others. There are no rules, other than those established by the Senate itself, for how this should work.

The word orotund is a good one to know if you're going to be discussing rhetoric. It means: pompous, bombastic, or pretentious; marked by inflated grandeur and rant; (of speech) full-sounding, sonorous; (of writing) eloquent, powerful, or grandiloquent. The word comes from Latin ōrōtundus "elaborate in style," from ōrō "speak out loud." The prefix ōr– also appears in the words orator and oration, which are both related to speaking or public speaking. The suffix –undus can be found in other English words, including redundant, abhorrent, and pellucid.

The llanos region of Venezuela is the largest tropical grassland in South America. It contains a variety of ecosystems: savannahs, wetlands, gallery forests, rivers and lakes. But it also has one of the highest rates of deforestation on the continent. The main cause of this destruction is overgrazing by cattle, which are often left to wander freely across the plains. This problem is exacerbated by drought, caused by El Niño weather patterns that have increased as a result of climate change. The combination of these factors led to the 2014/5 food crisis in Venezuela, when the government was unable to feed its people due to falling production of basic staples such as corn, rice, sugarcane and coffee.

The hippocampus belongs to a larger group of structures called the limbic system, which is involved in emotion and memory formation. A large body of research has implicated the hippocampus as being crucial for declarative (conscious) memory. In humans, declarative memories are typically factual knowledge or autobiographical events. Damage to the hippocampus usually leads to amnesia, that is, loss of memories formed after the damage occurred. Aissam Dam, an 11 year old boy in France, was born deaf. Recently he underwent a procedure that allowed him to hear sound for the first time. Aissam had been diagnosed with Usher syndrome type III which is caused by a genetic mutation that affects hearing and vision. This condition causes progressive loss of both senses, starting with hearing at birth and then vision later in life. He received a new gene therapy treatment called GENEVESTIGATE that was developed by GenSight Biologics. The treatment uses viruses to deliver a correct copy of the USH3A gene into cells inside the inner ear. Doctors are hopeful that this new technique will help other patients with similar conditions.

In early January, The New York Times published a column by Eduardo Porter entitled “We’re All Climate Economists Now,” which argues that the most important aspect of climate change is its economic impact. Porter is not wrong; the costs of climate change are enormous and should be front-and-center in our discussions on what to do about it. But the focus on economics has a major flaw: it ignores the fact that we have the technology to solve the problem, and that these technologies will also boost the economy. In other words, we don’t need to choose between solving climate change and a strong economy—we can have both at once.

The Israeli military has been given the green light to shoot down any Iranian drones that infiltrate its airspace, a senior Israel Defense Forces official said on Wednesday. The comments come after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his security cabinet held a meeting last week to discuss the threat posed by the Islamic Republic's unmanned aerial vehicles. According to the IDF official, who spoke anonymously with Reuters, the decision was made as part of a new policy designed to deal with potential threats from Iran, including drone attacks. "If there is another (Iranian) drone, it will be shot down," he told the news agency.
